site_description: Power systems engineering meets data science and AI
author: Bin Bian (Kevin)

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.text:
Every other case study on this page — grid analytics, cable thermal rating, sheath voltage validation, LLM grading benchmarks — was built and runs on **EmptyOS**. So before going deeper into any of them, here's the platform itself.

EmptyOS is a personal AI operating system. The premise: an OS is just a human doing things — reading, writing, thinking, searching. AI is one more provider of those capabilities, not a separate product. A markdown vault is the hard drive. Apps are atoms. The value is in the connections between them.

Open source. Self-hostable. **Live demo** (sample vault, sign-in token included — public sandbox, don't put real data in it). **Source on GitHub**.

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.text:
The 9 capabilities

think · read · write · search · speak · listen · draw · animate · see

Every app uses these via self.(). Providers (Ollama, OpenAI, Claude, ComfyUI, Whisper, edge-tts, OpenCV) plug into capabilities at startup with a priority order. If a provider is offline, the chain falls back to the next. Apps don't know which provider answered — they just got the result.

The same pattern handles the human-in-the-loop case: the **human is always the final fallback**. If no AI provider is available for think, the system asks me. That's what makes the *with you, not for you* posture load-bearing rather than rhetorical.

Apps as atoms

A new app is one manifest TOML + one app.py. Apps emit events; other apps subscribe by event name, not by import. The dependency graph IS the topology page — /topology renders it live from kernel state, not from a doc.

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.section: What this gets me as an engineer
chunks.text:
1. Cross-project compounding

Every case study on this portfolio is a directory under apps/ or apps/personal/. Building one new piece often costs one new app, because the platform already provides:

- a vault for durable state (markdown, frontmatter — git-friendly, model-friendly)
- an event bus to wire it to existing apps without modifying them
- a frontend kit (theme, component library, design tokens) — pages take an hour, not a day
- a job queue for GPU work
- a test harness (pytest + Playwright system tests + dogfood week-in-the-life tests)
- LLM provider routing with cost / quality / privacy tradeoffs already wired

The grid-analytics chain is ten apps. Building app #10 took the morning, not the week — because apps #1–9 were already there to talk to.

2. Privacy posture I can defend

Three modes (local, private, public), set in emptyos.toml. Every cloud provider is is_cloud=True and runs through a consent gate before invocation; vault content never goes to cloud by default unless an app opts in per-request. The same codebase runs on a laptop with full local LLMs, on a Tailscale-private machine, or on a public VPS with a token.

For an energy / utility context: vault stays on-disk, can be physically air-gapped, every external network call is consent-gated. The security review surface is the kernel's capability chain — not 60 apps each making their own decision.

3. AI as a capability, not a product

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.section: What this gets me as an engineer
chunks.text:
This is the part that compounds with my engineering background. Every analytics app — cable rating, grid twin, hosting capacity — has the same hooks for "explain this", "suggest the next step", "rank these for me", "summarise across the fleet". I write the analytics once; the AI surface drops in via self.think() with no app-side wiring.

When a customer enquiry needs *"can Acme Solar add 15 kW at pole T-05?"*, the same capability chain that runs the physics model also writes the customer response. One platform, one privacy boundary, one place to swap providers when something better lands.

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.section: How it shows up in the other case studies
chunks.text:
- **Grid Analytics Chain** — ten apps wired via the kernel event bus, validation framework reused from cable thermal rating, LLM-cached responses for deterministic demos.
- **Cable thermal rating + sheath voltage validation** — 600+ pytest tests run against the same harness EmptyOS uses for its own apps. Validation framework (MAE / RMSE / bias / 95% CI / divergent assets) is reused unchanged across cable, twin, and pricing case studies.
- **LLM-MCQ benchmarking + AI essay grading** — share the LLM provider chain and prompt-as-artifact convention. Every prompt is a named module-level constant with system / user separation, temperature bands per task type.
- **Fuel price forecasting** — runs as an EmptyOS app; the streaming chart + statistical bands + scenario panel are built from the same shared frontend kit as everything else.

The platform isn't a side project that distracts from the engineering work. It's what makes the engineering work compound.

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.text:
- **It's mine.** Built to my taste, my workflow, my vault structure. Self-hostable, but not zero-config — emptyos.toml has knobs. Documented (the system writes its own docs from manifests via eos app info), but it's not a turn-key SaaS replacement.
- **Local-first means local-cost.** Running everything on your own hardware costs hardware. The provider chain is designed so cloud LLMs slot in for the parts where local quality isn't enough — but the privacy default is local.
- **Apps are atoms, not microservices.** They share a process, a kernel, a vault. Scale-out story is "run another EmptyOS instance with a different vault" — federation, not horizontal sharding. Right tradeoff for personal / team use; not a fit if you want one global instance with thousands of users.

chunks.title: EmptyOS — The Platform Behind These Case Studies
chunks.text:
- Plugin marketplace surface — today plugins are folders under plugins/; a manifest registry would let third parties contribute without forking.
- Multi-vault federation for team use — same kernel, multiple mounted vaults with per-vault capability scopes.
- More energy-flavoured app pack — DER hosting calculator, protection coordination assistant, BESS dispatch optimiser. Each one is "another app" in the sense that grid-analytics was.

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
Cable sheath standing voltage — the voltage induced on a single-point-bonded cable sheath by the main conductor current — is a safety-critical quantity. If the standing voltage exceeds the sheath-to-earth insulation rating, the sheath insulation punctures; if it exceeds the personnel touch-voltage limit, accessible cable ends become hazardous.

Utilities worldwide rely on commercial cable design software (closed-source, proprietary) to calculate this value. But the underlying physics is public — it's published in three major standards (CIGRE TB 283 / TB 347, IEEE 575-2014 Annex F, IEC 60287). And here's the thing: **those standards don't quite agree with each other**. Each makes a different choice about the "effective radius" in the coaxial self-mutual impedance term, which turns out to be the dominant source of spread between methods.

This project answered a specific question: **when an engineer implements the published formulations in Python, how closely does each one match the commercial reference — and which one is the safe default?**

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
Reference Setup

- **Cable**: 1C 132 kV 2000 mm² Cu Milliken conductor, XLPE insulation, Al corrugated sheath (conductor Ø 56.2 mm, sheath 50.0 / 62.0 mm, overall diameter 137.6 mm)
- **Reference tool**: industry-standard commercial cable design software — closed-source, used by most major utilities
- **12 real-world test cases** drawn from actual project designs:
 - BORING_2M — horizontal directional drill, 2000 mm phase spacing
 - FLAT_400MM, FLAT_650MM — flat formation, tight and medium spacing
 - B1_2500mm, B9_3000mm — single-circuit wide spacing
 - B2–B8 — two-circuit bundled installations, 350–600 mm phase spacing with various circuit-to-circuit offsets
- **Operating currents**: 1310 A (9 cases) and 1500 A (3 cases); sheaths single-point-bonded, flat formation, dual circuit

Six Algorithm Variants

All six are **analytical formulations implemented in Python** (no simulation time-stepping, no iteration). They differ in how they evaluate the self-mutual coaxial impedance term Z = jωμ₀/(2π) · ln(De/r). The key parameter is **what radius r represents**:

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
| # | Algorithm | Source | Radius choice |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CIGRE 283 De-method — area r | CIGRE TB 283 / TB 347 | r = equivalent area radius (25.23 mm) |
| 2 | CIGRE 283 De-method — phys r | CIGRE TB 283 / TB 347 | r = physical conductor outer radius (28.10 mm) |
| 3 | Image method — area r | Classical mirror-image | r = equivalent area radius |
| 4 | Image method — phys r | Classical mirror-image | r = physical conductor outer radius |
| 5 | IEEE 575 De-method — GMR | IEEE 575-2014 Annex F | r = sheath GMR √(r_in · r_out) = 55.68 mm |
| 6 | Image method — GMR | Classical + IEEE radius | r = sheath GMR |

Grouped, the 6 variants are **2 base methods (CIGRE De-method, Image method) × 3 radius choices (area, physical, sheath GMR)**. The standards don't disagree on the underlying physics — they disagree on the bookkeeping.

Tech Stack

- **Python**: numpy, pandas, dataclasses for cable-geometry modelling
- **opendssdirect.py**: EMT-style OpenDSS 6-conductor cable model as a secondary cross-check
- **Validation harness**: 72 comparison points (12 cases × 6 algorithms) auto-tabulated with per-case and per-algorithm statistics
- **Streamlit UI**: interactive parameter sweeps for engineers exploring the cable design space

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
Physical Radius Beats Area Radius — Consistently

Across both the CIGRE De-method and the Image method, swapping the equivalent-area radius for the physical conductor outer radius cut mean error roughly in half:

| Base method | Area r | Phys r |
|---|---|---|
| CIGRE 283 De-method | +9.31% | +5.79% |
| Image method | +7.89% | **+4.36%** |

The best overall variant — **Image method with physical conductor radius** — matched the reference within a 4.4% mean error and a per-case range of [−12.1%, +1.4%]. For this cable family, the reference software is better approximated by physical-radius Image theory than by any of the other five formulations.

IEEE 575 (GMR) Under-Predicts — Consistently

The two variants using **sheath GMR as the effective radius** (IEEE 575-2014 Annex F formulation) produced a **consistent −16% to −18% bias** vs the reference. The standard deviations tell an interesting story:

- IEEE 575 De-method (GMR): mean **−16.48%**, std **0.05%**
- Image method (GMR): mean **−17.98%**, std **3.96%**

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
A std of 0.05% across 12 diverse cases isn't random scatter — it's a **deterministic offset**. The IEEE formulation produces repeatable answers that are consistently lower than the reference. If the reference is right, IEEE 575 under-protects the design; if IEEE 575 is right, the reference is conservative by a similar margin. Either way, an engineer picking "the IEEE method" without cross-checking would size sheath insulation ~17% lower than the commercial tool would recommend — a safety-relevant gap.

Error Depends on Geometry

All six algorithms handled wide-spacing, single-circuit configurations well. BORING_2M (2000 mm spacing), B1_2500mm, B9_3000mm — the top methods stayed within ±5% of the reference.

The hard cases were **tight-spacing multi-circuit bundles** — B2–B6 at 350 mm phase spacing with mutual-induction effects from the adjacent circuit. Per-case max errors reached 19–29%. This is consistent with the underlying physics: at close spacing, the ln(De/r) term becomes increasingly sensitive to the chosen radius, and cross-circuit mutuals amplify any formulation-level bias.

Conservative vs Non-Conservative

A safety-relevant view: how often does each algorithm land on the conservative side (prediction ≥ reference)?

- **CIGRE De-method** (both radii): **9 / 12** cases above reference — conservative for design sizing
- **Image method — phys r**: 4 / 12
- **Image method — area r**: 5 / 12
- **IEEE 575 GMR + Image GMR**: **0 / 12** — consistently below reference

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
For safety-critical sheath-voltage sizing, a non-conservative algorithm is the worst failure mode: the engineer believes the design is safe, but real voltages are higher. The **CIGRE variants give the most design headroom**; the **IEEE GMR formulations give the least**. An engineer using IEEE 575 as a standalone check would never land on the safe side — which strongly suggests pairing it with at least one CIGRE check when the margin matters.

Thermal Independence Verified

A sanity check: cases with **identical electromagnetic geometry but different soil thermal resistivity, burial depth, or daily load factor** (B3/B5/B6 and B4/B7 groups) produced **exactly identical sheath voltages** across all six algorithms — bit-for-bit. This confirms the sheath-voltage calculation is properly decoupled from the thermal model. Thermal inputs shouldn't influence pure electromagnetic induction, and in this implementation they don't.

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
The core insight: the "6 algorithms" aren't six independent physics models — they're a **2 × 3 grid** of (base method) × (effective radius). Encoding that factorisation directly made the whole sweep a handful of lines and kept the comparison table honest:

One small invariance test — assert solve(geom, soil_rho=1) == solve(geom, soil_rho=2.5) — locks in that the electromagnetic calculation can never accidentally couple to thermal parameters. Three lines of pytest; outlives five refactors.

chunks.title: Cable Sheath Voltage Modelling — Validating Open-Source Algorithms Against Industry Software
chunks.text:
- **Standards disagree on bookkeeping, not physics.** The 16–18% spread between CIGRE and IEEE 575 variants isn't a bug in either standard — it's a consequence of different radius conventions in the same underlying ln(De/r) term. An engineer using commercial software needs to know which convention it internally implements to interpret its results correctly.
- **Physical radius approximates the reference better than GMR.** At least for this cable family, the commercial tool behaves more like a physical-radius Image method than like IEEE 575's GMR formulation.
- **Consistent bias ≠ random error.** IEEE 575 GMR's std of 0.05% across 12 diverse cases means the offset is deterministic, not noise. That's actionable: if operational constraints require using IEEE 575, a correction factor (or mandatory paired CIGRE check) should accompany it.
- **A validation framework catches standard-ambiguity that single calculations miss.** Without running all 6 against the reference, an engineer picking one method off the shelf would quietly under- or over-estimate sheath voltage by up to 17% — a safety-relevant error that no individual calculation would ever surface. Having a multi-algorithm harness turns "which standard is right?" from an opinion into a number.

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
A volunteer-based emergency relief organisation managing disaster response across a regional area relied entirely on basic web-based Google Spreadsheets for critical operations — tracking affected individuals, coordinating volunteers, matching resources to needs, and managing triage workflows.

While functional for small incidents, this approach created serious bottlenecks during large-scale events:
- **Inefficient cross-referencing** between volunteer databases and affected persons records
- **Manual resource matching** causing delays when speed is critical
- **Limited collaboration** between triage, operations, and logistics teams working simultaneously
- **No audit trail** for decisions made during high-pressure situations
- **Data integrity risks** from concurrent spreadsheet edits

The goal: identify and recommend an IT solution that streamlines operations, enhances coordination, and improves disaster response efficiency — within the budget and technical constraints of a volunteer organisation.

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
Methodology & Frameworks
1. **Stakeholder Interviews** — Conducted structured interviews with two key operational staff to capture workflows, pain points, and aspirations
2. **MoSCoW Prioritisation** — Categorised 20+ requirements into Must-Have, Should-Have, Could-Have, and Won't-Have
3. **BPMN Process Modelling** — Created As-Is and To-Be process diagrams for four core operational workflows
4. **ISO/IEC 25010 Evaluation** — Applied product quality standards (functionality, usability, reliability, security, compatibility, maintainability, flexibility) as evaluation criteria
5. **Quantitative Scoring** — Weighted evaluation matrix comparing 7 solutions against all requirements
6. **Proof-of-Concept Testing** — Built and tested a demo system with 81 test cases (95% pass rate)
7. **Phased Implementation Planning** — 5-phase deployment roadmap with risk mitigation

Requirements Gathered

**Must-Have:**
- User management (login, registration, access control)
- Centralised data management (volunteers, affected persons, requests/needs)
- Logistics matchmaker and resource prioritisation
- Multi-user collaboration with real-time updates
- Secure cloud storage with backup and recovery
- Audit logging and PDF report generation

**Should-Have:**
- Multi-factor authentication
- Map support for geographic coordination
- Self-registration for volunteers
- User-friendly interface (minimal training required)

**Could-Have:**
- Mobile compatibility
- Future scalability and adaptability

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
Solutions Evaluated

| Solution | Type | Est. Cost (AUD) | Strengths | Verdict |
|----------|------|-----------------|-----------|---------|
| **Airtable** | SaaS | $7,000 | Flexible, affordable, user-friendly | Recommended |
| WebEOC | Commercial | $50,000+ | Comprehensive, real-time comms | Over-budget |
| NocoDB | Open-source | $7,150 | Customisable, low cost | Requires IT staff |
| Engel System | Open-source | $10,800 | Strong volunteer management | Lacks request tracking |
| D4H | Commercial | N/A | Equipment management | Too complex |
| Veoci | Commercial | N/A | Data analysis focus | Lacks logistics |
| DisasterLAN | Commercial | $15,000+/yr | Incident management | Limited AU presence |

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
Process Transformation (BPMN)

**As-Is Process** (4 workflows identified):
1. Immediate Response → manual volunteer mobilisation, spreadsheet-based coordination
2. Registration & Triage → manual data entry, paper-to-spreadsheet transcription
3. Assessment → human-only prioritisation, no system support
4. Resource Matching → manual lookup across multiple spreadsheets

**To-Be Process** (system-assisted):
1. Automated volunteer database with role-based access
2. Self-registration forms for both volunteers and affected persons
3. System-assisted prioritisation with scoring logic
4. Automated matching dashboard with real-time updates

Testing Results

- **81 test cases** executed across all functional modules
- **95% pass rate** (77/81 passed)
- 4 minor issues identified (input validation edge cases, display inconsistencies)
- All Must-Have requirements validated as functional

Recommendation: Airtable
Selected for the optimal balance of functionality, cost, and usability:
- Centralised data management with customisable tables and views
- Built-in automation for real-time updates
- API integration capability for future expansion
- $7,000 implementation cost (7x cheaper than enterprise alternatives)
- Minimal IT dependency (critical for volunteer organisations)
- 99.9% uptime SLA with automatic backups

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
Implementation Roadmap (5 Phases)
1. **Software Introduction** — Account setup, core training, documentation
2. **Database Design** — Table structure, field relationships, view configuration
3. **Data Migration** — Google Sheets → Airtable with integrity verification
4. **Testing & Training** — Operational testing, department-specific training
5. **Full Deployment** — Organisation-wide rollout, feedback loops, continuous improvement

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
Deliverables Produced
- **Requirements Analysis Report** — Stakeholder interview findings, MoSCoW categorisation
- **Business Process Diagrams** — BPMN As-Is and To-Be for 4 core workflows
- **Software Market Analysis** — 7-solution comparison with weighted scoring matrix
- **Testing Report** — 81 test cases with pass/fail results and issue tracking
- **Implementation Guide** — Phased roadmap, ER diagrams, access control policies, training plan
- **Demo System** — Pre-built Airtable workspace validated against all Must-Have requirements

Evaluation Framework
The ISO/IEC 25010 evaluation framework ensured systematic comparison:
- Each of 7 quality characteristics scored 1-5 per solution
- Weighted by MoSCoW priority (Must-Have criteria weighted 3x vs Could-Have)
- Total weighted scores compared across all 7 solutions
- Airtable scored highest overall despite not being the most feature-rich option — cost-effectiveness and usability compensated for feature gaps

chunks.title: Emergency Response System Analysis — IT Capstone Project
chunks.text:
- **Requirements gathering is the highest-leverage activity** — the two stakeholder interviews shaped everything downstream. Getting the right questions asked early saved weeks of rework
- **MoSCoW prioritisation forces honest trade-offs** — when the "Must-Have" list is honest, the evaluation almost runs itself. Most solutions were eliminated by failing a single Must-Have
- **Cost-effectiveness beats feature richness for volunteer organisations** — the $50,000 enterprise solution scored higher on raw features but was impractical. The right solution isn't the most capable one — it's the one that actually gets deployed
- **Proof-of-concept testing builds stakeholder confidence** — the 95% pass rate on 81 test cases converted skeptical volunteers into advocates before full deployment
- **BPMN diagrams communicate across skill levels** — visual process flows were the single most effective communication tool with non-technical stakeholders

chunks.title: AI Chatbot Platform Evaluation & Integration
chunks.text:
A B2B software company needed to add AI-powered customer support to their product website. The existing support relied on email and manual responses, creating delays and inconsistent service quality. The challenge was threefold:

1. **Platform selection** — Which chatbot solution best fits a technical product with complex documentation?
2. **Knowledge base population** — How to feed hundreds of product pages into the chatbot's training data automatically?
3. **Integration quality** — How to embed the widget seamlessly without degrading the existing website experience?

chunks.title: AI Chatbot Platform Evaluation & Integration
chunks.text:
Multi-Platform Evaluation

Evaluated 4 chatbot platforms against 12 criteria over a 3-month period:

| Criteria | Weight | Evaluation Method |
|----------|--------|-------------------|
| AI accuracy on domain questions | High | 50 test queries per platform |
| Widget customisation | Medium | CSS override testing |
| Human handoff capability | High | Live scenario testing |
| Knowledge base management | High | Content ingestion testing |
| Pricing vs feature ratio | Medium | TCO analysis |
| Cross-page session persistence | Medium | Multi-page navigation test |
| Analytics & reporting | Low | Dashboard review |
| Email capture & follow-up | Medium | Workflow testing |

Sitemap-to-Knowledge Pipeline

Built a Python tool to automatically extract and structure website content for chatbot training:

Two versions built iteratively:
- **v1** — Streamlit web UI for quick exploration and filtering
- **v2** — Tkinter desktop app with batch export, last-modified tracking, and CSV output for bulk upload to chatbot knowledge base

Website Integration

Designed a clean integration pattern:
- Lightweight JavaScript widget loaded asynchronously (no render blocking)
- CSS overrides for brand-consistent styling (colours, fonts, positioning)
- Custom announcement messages with configurable triggers
- Session limiting to prevent conversation sprawl
- Graceful fallback when widget CDN is unavailable

chunks.title: AI Chatbot Platform Evaluation & Integration
chunks.text:
Chat Volume Growth
After deployment, the chatbot handled an average of 45 conversations per week, with 72% resolved without human handoff — significantly reducing support ticket volume.

Platform Selection Decision
The winning platform scored highest on AI accuracy (domain-specific questions about technical software) and knowledge base management. The runner-up had stronger analytics but weaker AI responses for technical content.

Knowledge Pipeline Efficiency
The sitemap extraction tool processed 340+ URLs in under 10 seconds, generating structured content suitable for bulk upload. The last-modified tracking feature enabled incremental updates — only changed pages re-ingested.

Key Integration Learnings
- Widget load time impacted bounce rate — async loading was critical
- Custom CSS overrides needed testing across 5 browser/device combinations
- Announcement message timing (5s delay) balanced attention with non-intrusiveness

chunks.title: AI Chatbot Platform Evaluation & Integration
chunks.text:
Architecture

Tools Built
1. **Sitemap Extractor v1** — Streamlit app for interactive URL exploration with filtering
2. **Sitemap Extractor v2** — Tkinter desktop app with batch processing, incremental tracking, Excel/CSV export
3. **Mock Test Site** — HTML pages simulating production website for isolated widget testing
4. **Chat Analytics Processor** — CSV aggregation for daily/weekly/monthly conversation metrics

chunks.title: AI Chatbot Platform Evaluation & Integration
chunks.text:
- **Multi-platform evaluation needs structured methodology** — gut feeling leads to wrong choices. The scoring matrix revealed that the "prettiest" platform scored lowest on the criteria that actually mattered (AI accuracy, knowledge base management)
- **Data pipelines for AI are undervalued** — the sitemap extraction tool took 2 days to build but saved weeks of manual content copying. Most chatbot implementations fail not because of the AI but because of poor knowledge base population
- **Widget integration is UX engineering** — a chatbot that loads slowly, covers content, or looks foreign to the site does more harm than no chatbot at all. The CSS customisation and async loading pattern were as important as the AI configuration
- **Build tools for the next iteration** — the incremental update feature (last-modified tracking) meant content changes were reflected in the chatbot within hours, not days. Designing for ongoing maintenance was more valuable than the initial deployment

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
During the same emergency-response capstone that produced the *Emergency Response System Analysis* case study — and, a year later, the *BPMN for AI Agent Workflows* write-up — one question kept surfacing: *what would the victim-facing side look like if the intake desk had an AI?*

In a rescue-centre walk-in scenario, a volunteer at the intake desk has to capture the same five fields from every person: **name, address, phone number, type of assistance needed, and whether the person authorises phone contact**. Under pressure, with untrained volunteers, using a spreadsheet, this is where the workflow breaks down first — inconsistent fields, missing phone consent, transcription errors.

The prototype explored a specific narrow question: **can a small open-weight model (Mistral 7B) hold a short, focused, field-gathering conversation well enough to produce clean structured output for a downstream system?**

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
Your browser does not support video. Download MP4

Original capstone recording, 1 April 2024 — Streamlit UI over Mistral 7B, intake conversation through to the JSON summary. Mistral 7B was state-of-the-art open-weight at the time; the prompt-design and validate-and-retry patterns below still apply, but a modern small model (e.g. Mistral Small 3, Llama 3.3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B) would handle the schema-vs-instance problem out of the box.

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
Prompt design — two iterations

The system prompt went through a deliberate rewrite.

**v1 (2024-03-26)** used nested if/then logic:

> …ask the user to provide a name; if you already have the name, say the name and ask the user's address; if you have the name and address, ask the user's needs…

It worked, but it encoded the conversation state into prose — brittle, and the model sometimes lost track mid-conversation.

**v2 (2024-03-30)** flattened that into a numbered list of fields plus two explicit behaviour rules:

> 1. Name · 2. Address · 3. Phone Number · 4. Type of Assistance Needed · 5. Authorization for Phone Contact (Yes/No)
>
> If you already have some information, confirm what you know and only ask for the missing pieces. Once you have all details, provide a summary table.

Same intent, but the model now treats the fields as a checklist rather than a linear script. Adding **Authorization for Phone Contact** as an explicit field was the other change — in an emergency intake, tacit consent isn't good enough.

Two conversation shapes, one chatbot

The same prompt had to handle two very different user behaviours:

**Multi-round (the nervous-person case)** — one field at a time, with the bot naming what it has and asking for what's missing:

> **User:** morning
> **Bot:** Good morning! May I please have your name…
> **User:** Kevin
> **Bot:** Thank you, Kevin. Now, may I please have your address…

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
**One-shot (the organised-person case)** — the user dumps everything in a single sentence, and the bot extracts fields without asking again:

> **User:** My name is Kevin, I live at para hills, I need some food.
> **Bot:** *[extracts name, address, need in one pass and confirms]*

The important part: the same system prompt does both. No mode switching, no dual prompts. The LLM reads what's already known and adapts.

JSON extraction — catching the "schema-instead-of-instance" bug

Turning the conversation into a database row meant asking the model for a JSON object matching a Pydantic schema (name, address, need). This is where Mistral 7B's limits showed up.

Some responses returned the **schema itself** instead of an instance:

A smaller model occasionally confuses "give me something shaped like this" with "give me this". Rather than prompt-engineering around it, the fix was a **retry layer**: PydanticOutputParser validates the output; a malformed instance triggers a re-ask. Then a second simplification layer wraps the model to keep only the JSON block.

This pattern — **validate, reject, retry** — is more robust than trying to make the model perfect. It also made the cost of a weaker model acceptable.

Deployment

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
- **Chainlit** UI first, for fast iteration on the conversation itself
- **Streamlit** UI next, for a version that matched the rest of the capstone team's demos
- **Amazon Bedrock** for serving Mistral 7B — took the local-dev prototype to a setup that other team members could hit without a local GPU
- **Gretel** for generating synthetic intake dialogues, to stress-test the conversation beyond the handful of real cases a student team can script

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
- **Conversation works in both shapes** — one-field-at-a-time and one-shot, without a mode flag
- **Five fields collected reliably** after the v2 prompt rewrite, including the phone-contact authorization
- **Malformed JSON handled** via Pydantic validation + retry — the prototype is tolerant of Mistral 7B's occasional schema confusion
- **Deployed end-to-end** — Mistral on Bedrock, Streamlit front-end, synthetic test data from Gretel

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
This was an exploratory prototype inside a larger capstone, and one branch was left open:

- **Matching needs to resources** — connecting the extracted need field to an inventory/volunteer database so the bot could say *"we have food at the Para Hills centre, 10 minutes away"*. The capstone's final recommendation ended up being an Airtable deployment for the volunteer organisation, and the chatbot stayed a proof-of-concept.

The later *BPMN for AI Agent Workflows* post is, in a sense, the next step: treating intake, classification, urgency assessment, and dispatch as separate agents rather than one monolithic chatbot. This prototype was the single-agent baseline that motivated that redesign.

chunks.title: Emergency Response Intake Chatbot — Mistral 7B Prototype
chunks.text:
- **Flattening a prompt beats scripting it** — the v1→v2 rewrite from nested if/then to a numbered field list was a bigger win than any model swap
- **One prompt, two conversation shapes** — modern chat models can handle both drip-feed and one-shot input from the same system prompt; I don't need to branch the code
- **Validate-and-retry is cheaper than prompt-perfecting** — for a 7B model, Pydantic-based rejection catches the malformed cases faster than trying to make the prompt airtight
- **Explicit consent is a prompt concern** — "ask for phone authorization" needed to be a numbered field, not a footnote, for the model to reliably collect it
- **A single-agent intake bot has a ceiling** — once you want classification, urgency, and dispatch, one LLM juggling all of it gets fragile. The next design iteration split those roles across agents

chunks.title: Australian Fuel Price Analysis — Time Series Pattern Detection
chunks.text:
Australian retail fuel prices exhibit complex patterns — seasonal cycles, supply shocks, regional variations, and correlation with international crude oil benchmarks. Understanding these patterns is essential for energy market analysis, consumer policy, and demand forecasting.

The challenge: given 5 years of weekly fuel pricing data across 8 Australian cities, can we systematically identify pricing cycles, detect anomalies, and quantify the relationship between international crude oil markets and domestic retail prices?

chunks.title: Australian Fuel Price Analysis — Time Series Pattern Detection
chunks.text:
Data Sources
- **Australian Institute of Petroleum (AIP)** — Weekly Trend Group Prices (TGP) for petrol and diesel across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth, Hobart, Darwin, and National Average (2019–2024)
- **Bloomberg/NYMEX** — WTI Crude Oil and Brent Oil Futures historical data
- **Singapore GASOIL PLATTS** — Diesel benchmark futures
- **FuelWatch** — Monthly retail price CSVs (72 files, 2019–2024)

Pipeline
1. **Data Ingestion**: Loaded multi-sheet Excel workbooks with pandas, parsed datetime indices, handled missing values across 5 years of weekly data
2. **Feature Engineering**: Extracted temporal components (year, month, day, weekday), computed rolling averages, calculated Cities Average and Major Cities Average aggregates
3. **Peak/Trough Detection**: Applied scipy.signal.find_peaks() at multiple temporal granularities — annual views, monthly breakdowns, and daily pricing points — to identify local maxima and minima
4. **Cross-Market Correlation**: Aligned Australian retail prices with Brent Crude and WTI futures on matching date indices to quantify price transmission lag and correlation strength
5. **Comparative Visualisation**: Multi-city overlays with colour-differentiated time series, dual-axis plots for national vs. city-level trends, annotated peak/trough markers

chunks.title: Australian Fuel Price Analysis — Time Series Pattern Detection
chunks.text:
Tech Stack
- **Python**: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy.signal
- **Data**: ~2,080 data points per city (5 years x ~52 weeks), 8 geographic series
- **Visualisation**: Time-series line plots (20x10 to 50x10 inch figures), comparative analysis plots, vertical dashed-line peak/trough markers

chunks.title: Australian Fuel Price Analysis — Time Series Pattern Detection
chunks.text:
Synchronised Price Movements
All 8 cities showed highly correlated price movements, suggesting national-level market drivers (crude oil imports, refinery margins, fuel excise) dominate over local supply factors. Regional variations existed but were bounded — typically within 10-15 cpl of the national average.

Seasonal Cycling Patterns
Peak detection revealed recurring annual patterns:
- **Price spikes** clustered around holiday periods and refinery maintenance windows
- **Trough periods** aligned with demand softening in winter months
- Year-on-year volatility comparison showed 2022 as an extreme outlier (Ukraine conflict impact on global oil markets)

Crude Oil Correlation

Petrol TGP showed strong positive correlation with Brent Crude futures, with an observable 2-4 week lag in price transmission from international benchmarks to Australian retail. Diesel showed similar but slightly weaker correlation with Singapore GASOIL PLATTS.

Regional Divergence
Perth and Darwin exhibited the highest variance from the national average, likely due to geographic isolation and different supply chain logistics compared to east-coast cities.

chunks.title: Australian Fuel Price Analysis — Time Series Pattern Detection
chunks.text: The analysis pipeline processed ~16,640 individual price observations (8 cities x 2,080 weekly records) with additional cross-referencing against 3 international benchmark series.

chunks.title: Australian Fuel Price Analysis — Time Series Pattern Detection
chunks.text:
- **Signal processing techniques transfer well to market data** — find_peaks from scipy, designed for signal processing, proved more robust for cycle detection than manual threshold-based approaches
- **Data alignment is critical for cross-market analysis** — matching weekly Australian TGP data against daily futures required careful resampling and forward-fill strategies
- **Visualisation scale matters** — large multi-city plots (50x10 inches) made patterns visible that were invisible at standard plot sizes; this informed later dashboard design decisions
- **Public data can be surprisingly rich** — AIP, FuelWatch, and Bloomberg together provided sufficient depth for meaningful time series analysis without any proprietary data

chunks.title: AI-Assisted Essay Grading — LLM Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
University essay grading is time-intensive — a single instructor may spend 60+ hours grading a cohort of 50 essays against multi-criteria rubrics. Can large language models reliably assist with this task?

This project built a production-ready pipeline to answer three questions:
1. **Can GPT grade essays** according to structured rubrics with multi-criteria scoring?
2. **Which model performs better** — GPT-3.5-turbo or GPT-4?
3. **What temperature setting** optimises agreement between AI and human graders?

chunks.title: AI-Assisted Essay Grading — LLM Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
Architecture

Prompt Engineering Strategies

Four template variations tested systematically:

1. **Multiple Criteria** — Standard: score each rubric criterion independently (0-100), weighted aggregation for final grade
2. **Only Grade** — Two-step: assign letter grades first (HD/D/C/P/F), then convert to numeric scores
3. **Feedback-First** — Generate personalised feedback before scoring (hypothesis: reasoning improves accuracy)
4. **Baseline Comparison** — Provide a reference essay scored at 70 to contextualise relative performance

Each template used LangChain's StructuredOutputParser to enforce JSON schema output with per-criterion numeric fields.

Temperature Experiment Design
- **Range**: 0.0 to 2.0 in 0.2 increments (11 test points)
- **Sample**: 45 essays per temperature setting
- **Metric**: Pearson correlation coefficient against human baseline grades
- **Token accounting**: cl100k_base encoding, per-message overhead tracking, automatic truncation for model context limits

Tech Stack
- **Backend**: Python 3.9, OpenAI API (0.27.6), LangChain (0.0.200)
- **Frontend**: Streamlit (1.23.1) with multi-tab workflow
- **Analysis**: statsmodels (OLS regression), seaborn/matplotlib
- **Extraction**: textract (PDF/DOCX parsing), tiktoken (token counting)
- **Deployment**: Docker containerisation → Azure Container Registry
- **Auth**: streamlit-authenticator for session-based access control

chunks.title: AI-Assisted Essay Grading — LLM Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
> **Note on figures:** The underlying essay dataset is student coursework held under an institutional data agreement. Numbers and charts in this section are **illustrative** — they reflect the shape and direction of the real findings but are not the actual study values.

Temperature Impact on Human-AI Agreement

| Temperature | Correlation (r) | Valid Samples | Notes |
|------------|-----------------|---------------|-------|
| 0.0 | N/A | full | Deterministic — zero variance |
| 0.2–0.6 | low, inconsistent | full | Weak positive signal |
| 0.8 | weak positive | full | First meaningful alignment |
| 1.0–1.4 | mixed | full | Regression toward noise |
| 1.6 | moderate positive | mostly full | Improved alignment |
| 2.0 | **highest observed** | reduced | Best correlation, but sample degradation from malformed outputs |

*Specific values suppressed — the exact per-temperature statistics are derived from confidential student work. Pattern and ordering are what the study established.*

**Key Insight**: Temperature = 0 produces constant outputs (meaningless for correlation). Higher temperatures (1.6–2.0) improved human-AI alignment but increased the rate of malformed outputs. The optimal operating point depends on the acceptable trade-off between agreement quality and output reliability.

chunks.title: AI-Assisted Essay Grading — LLM Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
Model Behaviour Patterns
- GPT tends toward **central tendency** — scores cluster around 70-80 regardless of actual essay quality
- Linear regression slopes consistently < 1.0, indicating the model compresses the score range compared to human graders
- GPT-4's extended context (8K tokens) reduced truncation artefacts for longer essays

Practical Recommendation
The system functions best as a **grading aid** (instructor review tool) rather than autonomous grader. Modest human-AI agreement means AI scores should flag outliers and suggest ranges, not replace human judgment — a finding that informed stakeholder communication.

chunks.title: AI-Assisted Essay Grading — LLM Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
Streamlit Application (6-Tab Workflow)
1. **Input New Data** — Upload rubric, assignment description, and submission ZIP
2. **Select Dataset** — Load previous grading sessions from directory structure
3. **Set Parameters** — Model selection, prompt template editor, save custom templates
4. **Advanced Settings** — Temperature range, loop count, test mode, output validation
5. **Run Grading** — Execute pipeline with progress tracking, cache API responses, export CSV
6. **Result Analysis** — Load human grades, compute correlations, generate regression plots

Token-Aware Processing

Docker Deployment

Deployed to Azure Container Registry with environment-injected API keys.

chunks.title: AI-Assisted Essay Grading — LLM Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
- **Prompt template design is the primary lever** — the difference between "score this essay" and "first explain your reasoning, then score" produced measurably different output distributions. Prompt engineering is software engineering
- **Statistical validation must match the use case** — Pearson correlation alone is insufficient; the central tendency bias was only visible through regression slope analysis
- **Temperature = 0 is not "most accurate"** — it's deterministic, which breaks correlation metrics entirely. This counterintuitive finding changed how I think about LLM evaluation methodology
- **Token economics matter at scale** — grading 45 essays across 11 temperature settings across 4 prompt templates generates thousands of API calls. Token counting, caching, and cost estimation are production requirements, not nice-to-haves
- **The "grading aid" framing was the right recommendation** — presenting weak correlation as "the model is useful for flagging outliers" rather than "the model can't grade" was the difference between stakeholder buy-in and project rejection

chunks.title: LLM Accuracy Benchmarking — Multi-Model MCQ Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
How accurately can large language models answer domain-specific multiple-choice questions? And does accuracy vary by subject domain, question difficulty, or model generation?

This project built an automated benchmarking pipeline to evaluate three generations of GPT models across 1,300+ MCQs spanning 10 subject domains — measuring not just overall accuracy but per-domain performance, question-level error patterns, and the effect of model scaling on correctness.

chunks.title: LLM Accuracy Benchmarking — Multi-Model MCQ Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
Pipeline Architecture

The system processes questions through four stages:

1. **Preprocessing** — Raw question banks (HTML-formatted with embedded answer options) are cleaned, deduplicated, and assigned unique IDs. Answer options are extracted and normalised to consistent A/B/C/D format
2. **Batch API Calling** — Questions are sent to OpenAI's API with retry logic, rate limiting, and incremental caching. Each model variant processes all questions independently
3. **Grading** — Model responses are compared against ground-truth answers at three levels: individual answer options (partial credit), whole questions (all-or-nothing), and quiz-level aggregation
4. **Analysis** — Per-domain accuracy rates, cross-model comparison, error pattern clustering

Models Evaluated
- **GPT-3** (text-davinci-003) — 175B parameters, instruction-tuned
- **GPT-3.5-turbo** — Chat-optimised, faster inference
- **GPT-4** — Largest model, strongest reasoning

Tech Stack
- **Python**: pandas, numpy, BeautifulSoup (HTML parsing)
- **API**: OpenAI ChatCompletion with retry/backoff
- **Data**: 1,319 unique MCQs from 10 domains, ~30,000 individual answer evaluations

chunks.title: LLM Accuracy Benchmarking — Multi-Model MCQ Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
> **Note on figures:** The underlying dataset is student coursework held under an institutional data agreement. All numbers and charts in this section are **illustrative** — they reflect the shape and pattern of the real findings but are not the actual study values.

Model Scaling Improves Accuracy

Each model generation showed measurable improvement in overall accuracy:
- GPT-3 averaged 62% correct across all domains
- GPT-3.5 improved to 71%, with strongest gains in reasoning-heavy subjects
- GPT-4 reached 84%, with near-human performance in factual recall domains

Domain-Specific Performance Varies Significantly

Performance was not uniform across subjects. Models performed best on factual/definitional questions and worst on questions requiring multi-step reasoning or contextual interpretation.

Error Pattern Analysis

The most common error patterns across all models:
- **Plausible distractor selection** — models chose the "second-best" answer 40% of the time when wrong
- **Negation blindness** — questions with "which is NOT" phrasing had 25% lower accuracy
- **Multi-concept questions** — questions requiring synthesis of two or more concepts showed the steepest accuracy drop

Caching and Resilience

The pipeline cached every API response incrementally, allowing interrupted runs to resume without re-querying. Total API cost for the full benchmark was tracked per model, demonstrating cost-efficiency awareness.

chunks.title: LLM Accuracy Benchmarking — Multi-Model MCQ Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text: The preprocessing stage handled HTML-embedded questions with nested formatting, extracting clean question text and answer options using BeautifulSoup with custom parsing rules for inconsistent input formats.

chunks.title: LLM Accuracy Benchmarking — Multi-Model MCQ Evaluation Pipeline
chunks.text:
- **Batch API design matters** — without incremental caching, a single network error at question 800 would waste the entire run. The cache-and-resume pattern saved significant time and cost
- **Multi-level scoring reveals different stories** — partial-credit scoring showed GPT-3.5 was closer to GPT-4 than all-or-nothing scoring suggested, because GPT-3.5 often got 3 of 4 options right
- **Negation is an LLM weakness** — the "which is NOT" pattern was the single strongest predictor of model failure, more than domain or difficulty level
- **Cost tracking is a production requirement** — knowing that the full benchmark cost $47 (GPT-3), $12 (GPT-3.5), or $180 (GPT-4) directly informed model selection recommendations

chunks.title: About
chunks.text: I'm **Bin Bian** — a power systems engineer building at the intersection of **energy infrastructure, data science, and AI**.

chunks.title: About
chunks.text:
I started in China designing 220kV transmission cable tunnels and high-voltage cable systems for the State Grid, where I led teams on underground cable projects and earned 7 patents in HV cable, BESS, and earthing design. I then moved to Australia to work across the full spectrum of power systems — from HV transmission to 11kV distribution to utility-scale BESS projects.

Along the way, I completed a Master of IT alongside my PhD in Electrical Engineering, picked up Python, and started building engineering calculation tools that evolved into a full AI-powered operating system.

chunks.title: About
chunks.text:
I don't just use data tools — I build them. And I don't just build software — I understand the engineering domain they serve.

- **Cable thermal rating calculator** implementing IEC 60287 with 2D/3D FEM analysis, 600+ automated tests
- **Sheath voltage analysis tool** validated against 12 CYMCAP reference cases across multiple algorithms
- **EmptyOS** — AI operating system with plugin architecture, event-driven design, and automated tests (pytest + Playwright); open source (GitHub · demo)
- **LLM evaluation pipelines** benchmarking GPT models on domain-specific tasks

That crossover — physics understanding combined with software delivery — is where the interesting things happen.
